title: Why a 'Significant' Discovery Can Still Be Wrong

source.title: Why Most Published Research Findings Are False

intro.summary: The paper asks a simple question: when a study reports a 'statistically significant' finding, how likely is that finding to be true? Ioannidis builds a simple counting model of a research field. The model tracks how many tested ideas are really true, how often studies catch real effects (power), how often they raise false alarms, how much bias pushes results toward 'positive', and how many teams chase the same question. Using this model with assumed numbers, he argues that in most study designs and fields a claimed finding is more likely false than true, especially in small, flexible, biased or 'hot' fields. The main limitation is that the key inputs, above all the share of tested ideas that are true, cannot be measured directly, so the conclusions depend on assumptions the author admits are 'considerably subjective'. Critics have argued that the headline 'most findings are false' depends on these assumed inputs, so it is best read as a warning about conditions, not a measured fact about every field. This lesson covers the core model, power, bias and multiple teams. It does not cover how later replication projects tested these ideas, Bayesian methods for setting prior odds, or detailed reforms such as preregistration; those are good next steps.
background: A study tests an idea, such as 'this drug lowers blood pressure', and a statistical test decides whether the data look convincing enough to claim an effect.
By convention, a result is called 'statistically significant' when it would happen less than 5% of the time if there were really no effect (p < 0.05).
Passing this test does not tell you the chance that the idea is true. That chance also depends on how plausible the idea was before the study.
A doctor's screening test is a useful everyday parallel: even an accurate test gives many false alarms when the disease is rare.
intro.aha: When many teams chase the same long-shot idea, the one 'significant' result that gets published can be hardly more likely true than the idea was before anyone studied it at all.
assumes: Type I and type II errors

primer.heading: The question
primer.body: Science news is full of findings that later fall apart: a diet that prevents cancer, a gene that causes a disease. Ioannidis asks whether this is bad luck or something built into how research is done and judged. His focus is the common habit of treating one study with p < 0.05 as proof that an effect is real.
primer.quote: There is increasing concern that most current published research findings are false.

primer.heading: What he did
primer.body: He did not run a new experiment. He built a simple model of a whole research field, like counting results in a big two-by-two table: ideas that are really true or not, against studies that say 'yes' or 'no'. The model has a few inputs: how many of the tested ideas are true to begin with, how good studies are at catching real effects, how often they raise false alarms, how much bias nudges results toward 'yes', and how many teams test the same question. He then plugged in plausible values for different kinds of research.

primer.heading: What he found
primer.body: In the model, a significant finding is often more likely false than true. Being significant is not enough: it matters how long a shot the idea was, how big and careful the study was, how much room researchers had to bend the analysis, and how many teams were racing. A large, careful trial of a plausible treatment does well, at about 85% true in his illustrative table. Exploratory work that searches thousands of genes does terribly.
primer.quote: Simulations show that for most study designs and settings, it is more likely for a research claim to be false than true.

primer.heading: The surprising part
primer.body: Some results run against intuition. If ten teams around the world test the same long-shot idea and one of them gets a significant result, that 'winning' result can be barely more believable than the idea was before anyone did any research. In fields where nothing is really there, the size of the claimed effects may simply measure how much bias the field has.

primer.heading: Why it matters, and its limits
primer.body: The paper pushed scientists toward larger studies, shared standards, registering studies in advance, and judging the whole body of evidence rather than a single exciting result. Its numbers are model outputs, not measurements. The share of true ideas in a field cannot be observed directly, so readers must make rough guesses about it, and the author says so openly.
primer.quote: Even though these assumptions would be considerably subjective, they would still be very useful in interpreting research claims and putting them in context.
primer.quote_where: How Can We Improve the Situation?

concepts.title: A test is a filter with two kinds of mistakes
concepts.idea: A significance test lets through a small share (α) of ideas with no real effect as false alarms, and catches only a share (the power, 1 − β) of ideas with a real effect.

predict.question: Picture a field where none of the 1,000 ideas it tests has a real effect. It uses the usual 5% false-alarm rate. About how many 'yes' results will it get, and how many of them are true?
options: None: with no real effects, the test has nothing to say yes to
About 50, and every one of them is a false alarm
About 800, because the test catches most effects
We can't say without knowing the catch rate
why: It feels as if a test should stay silent when nothing is there. But the false-alarm rate applies to ideas with no effect, so 5% of 1,000 still come out yes.
Right: all 1,000 ideas sit in the no-effect row, and 5% of them slip through. That gives about 50 yes results, and none of them is real.
The catch rate only applies to ideas with a real effect. This field has none, so the catch rate never comes into play.
The catch rate filters the real-effect row, and that row is empty here. Only the false-alarm rate matters, and we know it is 5%.

terms.means: A 'yes' from the test for an idea that has no real effect: a false alarm
A 'no' from the test for an idea that does have a real effect: a miss
The Type I error rate: the share of no-effect ideas that the test wrongly calls significant, usually 5%
The share of real effects the test catches, written 1 − β, where β is the share it misses

model.title: 1,000 tested ideas sorted by the truth and by the test's verdict
model.note: Teaching model: a fixed set of 1,000 tested ideas, 100 with a real effect and 900 without. Each box shows the expected count, so there is no chance variation and no bias. The numbers are illustrative, not the paper's data.

controls.label: False-alarm rate (share of no-effect ideas that get a yes)
Catch rate (share of real effects that get a yes)

steps.say: Each row is a pile of ideas that a field tests. The top row holds 100 ideas with a real effect. The bottom row holds 900 ideas with none.
Each column is the test's verdict: yes, meaning significant, or no. This box counts every yes.
This slider sets how often an idea with no effect still gets a yes. Watch the bottom-left box grow.
This slider sets how many of the real effects the test manages to catch.
Two sliders, four boxes. Let's put them back and see what each one means.

explore.prompt: Now you run the filter. Move both sliders and watch which row each one changes.

goals.text: Make false alarms outnumber the real effects the test catches, while the test still catches more than half of the real effects.
hints: Which mistake comes from the bigger row of ideas?
The no-effect row holds nine times as many ideas, so a small rise in the false-alarm rate adds a lot of false alarms. Leave the catch rate alone.
Each step of the false-alarm slider adds 9 false alarms. Keep going until they pass the 80 real effects being caught.

goals.text: Build a better filter: fewer than 20 false alarms, while the test still catches at least 90 of the 100 real effects.
hints: Each slider controls one row. You will need to move both.
To get fewer false alarms, lower the false-alarm rate. To catch more real effects, raise the catch rate.
False alarms are 900 times the false-alarm rate, so that rate has to fall below about 2.2%.

feedback.correct: Yes. The false-alarm rate filters only the no-effect ideas. When every tested idea has no effect, about 5% of them still come out 'yes', and every one of those is false.
feedback.incorrect: The two rates act on different rows. The catch rate only matters for ideas with a real effect. The false-alarm rate applies to every no-effect idea, even when nothing real is there. With 1,000 no-effect ideas, about 50 still pass.

steps.say: Start at the usual setting. Of the 900 ideas with no effect, 45 still get a yes. Each of these false alarms is called a false positive.
The share of no-effect ideas that slip through is called α, the Type I error rate. At 5%, 5% of 900 gives 45.
Now the top row. Of the 100 real effects, 80 get a yes. The share the test catches is its power, written 1 − β.
The other 20 real effects are missed. Each miss is a false negative, and β is the share missed, here 20%.
Raise α to 10%. False alarms double to 90. Notice that the real-effect row did not move at all: each slider filters only its own row.
Now picture a weak study whose power is only 30%. It catches just 30 of the 100 real effects and misses 70.
Look at the 'yes' column: 30 real finds and 90 false alarms. Both mistakes are small-sounding rates, but together they decide what a pile of 'yes' results is made of.

understand.explanation: A significance test works like a filter that sorts ideas into 'yes' and 'no'. It makes two kinds of mistake. Ideas with no real effect get through as false positives at rate α, the Type I error rate, usually 5%. Ideas with a real effect are caught only at a rate called the power, 1 − β, and the rest become false negatives. Each rate acts on its own row, so how many ideas sit in each row matters as much as the rates themselves. The paper builds its whole argument on this 2 × 2 table, which compares research findings against the true state of each relationship. The counts here are expected averages: in real studies, chance makes them wobble, and bias can push them further.
understand.quote: The probability of a study finding a true relationship reflects the power 1 - β (one minus the Type II error rate). The probability of claiming a relationship when none truly exists reflects the Type I error rate, α.
understand.quote_where: Section 'Modeling the Framework for False Positive Findings'

connect.caption: These are the 'yes' cells of the paper's 2 × 2 table (Table 1). Here c is the number of relationships tested (1,000 in the model), and R is the ratio of true to no relationships (1 to 9 in the model, giving 100 real and 900 none). The blue term is the power (the catch rate) and the orange term is α (the false-alarm rate). Each one scales only its own row.

concepts.recap: A test makes two mistakes: it lets through a share α of no-effect ideas as false alarms, and it misses a share β of real effects.

activities.title: Everyday filters, same four boxes
activities.prompt: Every yes-or-no detector makes the same two mistakes as a significance test. Put each outcome in its box.

groups.label: Real, detector says no (missed: false negative)
Not real, detector says yes (false alarm: false positive)
Not real, detector says no (correctly quiet)

cards.text: The smoke alarm goes off while you make toast, and there is no fire.
cards.feedback: Nothing is burning, but the alarm says yes. This is the kind of mistake α counts.

cards.text: A small fire starts in the basement, and the alarm stays silent.
cards.feedback: Something real was there and the detector said no. This is a miss, the kind β counts.

cards.text: There is a real kitchen fire, and the alarm sounds.
cards.feedback: A real effect, correctly flagged. The share of these among real fires is the alarm's power.

cards.text: An ordinary quiet evening: no fire, no alarm.
cards.feedback: Nothing there, and nothing flagged. Most no-effect cases land here.

cards.text: A home pregnancy test shows positive, but the person is not pregnant.
cards.feedback: The test says yes when nothing is there: a false positive.

cards.text: A drug really works, but a small study of it finds no significant effect.
cards.feedback: A real effect the test failed to catch. Small, weak studies make this mistake often.

cards.text: A metal detector beeps over a coin buried in the sand.
cards.feedback: Something real, and the detector said yes.

cards.text: A study of a sugar pill with no effect finds no significant difference.
cards.feedback: No real effect, and the test correctly stays quiet.

activities.takeaway: A false alarm can only come from things that are not real, and a miss can only come from things that are real. That is why each mistake belongs to one row of the table.

concepts.title: Long-shot ideas make 'yes' results unreliable
concepts.idea: The chance that a significant finding is true (PPV) depends heavily on the share of tested ideas that were true to begin with (the pre-study odds R).

terms.means: Of all the 'yes' results, the share that are real: the chance that a significant finding is true
How many ideas with a real effect a field tests for every idea with no effect, before any study is run

model.title: 1,000 tested ideas sorted by the truth and by the test's verdict
model.note: Teaching model: a fixed set of 1,000 tested ideas, and you choose how many have a real effect. Each box shows the expected count, so there is no chance variation, no bias and only one study per idea. It uses the same arithmetic as the paper's 2×2 table (Table 1). The numbers are illustrative, not the paper's data.

controls.label: False-alarm rate (share of no-effect ideas that get a yes)
Catch rate (share of real effects that get a yes)
Ideas with a real effect (out of 1,000)

outputs.label: Real ideas for each no-effect idea
Share of 'yes' results that are real

steps.say: Same table as last time: 1,000 tested ideas, sorted by whether the effect is real and by what the test said.
One new slider: how many of the 1,000 ideas truly have an effect. Watch the rows refill as it drops.
And one new box: of all the 'yes' results, what share are real. Keep an eye on it.

explore.prompt: Leave the test alone and change the mix of ideas going in, then try to rescue a field of long shots by changing the test.

goals.text: Without touching the test's two rates, find the tipping point: the largest number of real ideas at which false alarms still outnumber real discoveries (within a few ideas).
hints: Only one slider should move here: the one for how many ideas are real.
Lower it slowly and watch for the moment the 'No effect, test says yes' box becomes highlighted.
The flip happens somewhere between 50 and 60 real ideas. Find the last setting before the highlight switches off.

goals.text: Picture a field where only 2% of tested ideas are real. Change the test so that at least half of the 'yes' results are real.
hints: With so few real ideas, which kind of mistake is crowding the 'yes' column?
The catch rate is already high. The false alarms come from the 980 no-effect ideas, so shrink the share of them that get a yes.
You need a false-alarm rate well below 2%, or a lower false-alarm rate together with a higher catch rate.

predict.question: A lab screens 10,000 random chemicals for a cure, and perhaps 10 of them truly work. The test catches 80% of real cures and gives a false alarm for 5% of duds. One chemical comes back 'yes'. Roughly how likely is it to really work?
options: About 95%
About 80%
About 50%
Under 2%
why: Tempting because the false-alarm rate is 5%, but that is the share of duds that pass. It is not the share of passes that are real. About 500 duds pass, against about 8 real cures.
80% is the catch rate: the chance that a real cure gets a yes. The question asks the reverse, how many of the yeses are real, and that depends on how rare real cures are.
A yes is not a coin flip. With only 10 real cures among 10,000, the mix going in is so lopsided that false alarms far outnumber real finds.
Correct. About 8 real cures pass (80% of 10), and about 500 duds pass (5% of 9,990). So only about 8 of roughly 508 yeses are real, around 1.6%.

feedback.correct: Right. When real ideas are rare, even a good test yields far more false alarms than real finds: about 8 real cures among roughly 508 yeses here.
feedback.incorrect: You probably read one of the test's rates as the chance that a yes is true. Those rates describe what the test does to real ideas and to duds. How many yeses are real also depends on how rare real cures are, and here they are very rare.

steps.say: Start where we left off: 100 real ideas out of 1,000. The 'yes' column holds 80 real discoveries and 45 false alarms, so 64% of the yeses are real.
That share has a name: the PPV (positive predictive value). It is the chance that a 'yes' result is actually true.
Now picture a field that tests mostly sensible ideas, half of them real. You get 400 discoveries against 25 false alarms, and the PPV climbs to about 94%.
The number of real ideas a field tests for each no-effect idea is called the pre-study odds R. Here it is 500 to 500, so R = 1.
Now a field of long shots: 20 real ideas in 1,000, so R is about 0.02. Only 16 real discoveries, but 49 false alarms. The PPV falls to about 25%.
Notice what did not change: the test. It still gives 5% false alarms and catches 80% of real effects. Only the mix of ideas going in changed.
Push it to the extreme: one real idea in 1,000. At most one real discovery hides among about 50 false alarms. Under 2% of the yeses are real.

understand.explanation: The test was the same in every scene: 5% false alarms and an 80% catch rate. Only the mix of ideas going in, the pre-study odds R, changed. When real ideas are rare, the few real discoveries are swamped by false alarms from the huge pile of no-effect ideas, so the PPV (positive predictive value) falls even though every study was run correctly. Ioannidis uses a 2×2 table to show that PPV = (1 − β)R/(R − βR + α), so a finding is more likely true than false only when power × R is larger than α. In his genome example (Box 1), R is 1 in 10,000 and power is 60%, so a just-significant result raises the chance of truth about 12-fold, but only to 12 in 10,000. The catch is that R is rarely known, and the paper says researchers must make rough, admittedly subjective, estimates of it. This model also leaves out bias and repeated studies, which the paper shows lower the PPV further.
understand.quote: As shown above, the post-study probability that a finding is true (PPV) depends a lot on the pre-study odds (R). Thus, research findings are more likely true in confirmatory designs, such as large phase III randomized controlled trials, or meta-analyses thereof, than in hypothesis-generating experiments.

check.task: Keep the usual 5% false-alarm rate and give the test a perfect catch rate. Then find a field where, even so, fewer than half of the 'yes' results are real.
check.hint: With a perfect catch rate, the number of real discoveries equals the number of real ideas. Compare that with 5% of the no-effect ideas, then lower the number of real ideas until the false alarms win.
check.misconception: A significant result at p < 0.05 means the finding is 95% likely to be true. In fact, 5% is the share of no-effect ideas that pass. How many passes are real also depends on how rare real ideas are.

connect.caption: This is the paper's formula from its 2×2 table. PPV is the 'share of yes results that are real' box. (1 − β) is the catch rate slider (power). α is the false-alarm rate slider. R, the pre-study odds, is the 'real ideas for each no-effect idea' box, which the model computes as real ÷ (1,000 − real). The top of the fraction counts real discoveries; the bottom counts all yeses, real and false.

concepts.recap: The same test gives mostly trustworthy 'yes' results in a field of likely ideas, and mostly false alarms in a field of long shots.

concepts.title: Small studies, small effects, weaker findings
concepts.idea: Small studies and small effects lower a study's power, and lower power drags down the chance that a significant finding is true.

predict.question: Imagine a study so tiny, chasing an effect so faint, that its power falls all the way to 5%. That is the same as its false-alarm rate. If it reports a significant 'yes', what is the chance the finding is true?
options: 0%: every such finding is false
The same as before the study: the 'yes' tells you nothing new
50%: a coin flip
Still fairly high, because it passed the significance test
why: Tempting, since the study is so weak. But real effects still pass 5% of the time, so some 'yes' results are true. They just aren't any more common than before the study.
Correct. Real ideas and dead ends now pass equally often (5% each), so 'yes' results mix them in the same proportion they were tested. PPV = R/(R + 1), the pre-study chance.
A coin flip needs real and false ideas tested in equal numbers. Here PPV falls back to the starting odds, which is 50% only if R = 1.
This is the trap the paper warns about. A 'yes' only counts as evidence if real effects pass more often than dead ends. At 5% power, they don't.

terms.means: How many people (or mice, or genes) a study measures. Here it is the number of people in each group.
Too small for the effect it is hunting, so the study usually misses that effect even when it is real.

model.title: How often a 'yes' is true, as the study gets bigger or the effect gets fainter
model.note: Teaching model: power comes from a simple two-group test (two-sided, false-alarm rate 0.05), using the size of the real effect in standard-deviation units and the number of people per group. The chance a 'yes' is true uses the paper's no-bias formula for a single study. Bias and multiple teams are left out. The formula is the paper's. All slider settings and the resulting numbers are illustrative, not the paper's data.

controls.label: True ideas per false idea tested (R)

x.label: True ideas per false idea tested (R)

series.label: A study that catches 80% of real effects

steps.say: The solid curve shows the chance that a 'yes' result is true. Each spot along the bottom is a different field.
On the left are fields full of long shots. Further right, more of the tested ideas are real. The dot marks one field.
This slider sets how many people the study tests in each group. Shrink it and watch the curve sink.
This one sets how big the real effect is. Make it fainter and the curve sinks again.
The dashed curve is a solid study that catches 80% of real effects. Keep it in mind as a yardstick.

explore.prompt: Now you steer. Keep the field's odds where they are and work only with the study's size and the effect's size.

goals.text: The field only has small effects (size 0.2 or less). Make its 'yes' results true at least 4 times in 5, without changing the field's odds.
hints: The effect has to stay small. Which other slider raises power?
Make the study bigger and watch the power box. The chance a 'yes' is true climbs with it.
You need the study to catch roughly four in five real effects. That takes a few hundred people per group.

goals.text: Run a small study (30 people per group or fewer) whose 'yes' results are still true at least 3 times in 4, at the field's current odds.
hints: With so few people, what else could raise power?
A bigger real effect is easier to catch, even in a small study.
Keep the study small and push the effect well past the middle of its range.

feedback.correct: Right. When power drops to the false-alarm rate, real ideas and dead ends pass the test at the same rate. The 'yes' results then mix true and false ideas in exactly the proportion they were tested, so the chance stays at its pre-study level.
feedback.incorrect: You may have treated 'passed the test' as evidence in itself. A 'yes' only raises the chance an idea is true if real effects pass more often than dead ends. At 5% power they pass equally often, so the chance stays where it started: R/(R + 1).

steps.say: Start at 100 people per group and a moderate effect. The study catches about 56% of real effects; that is its power. A 'yes' here is true about 74% of the time.
The number of people a study measures is its sample size. Cut it to 20 per group. Power falls to about 16%, and a 'yes' is now true only about 44% of the time. It is more likely false than true.
Why? False alarms don't shrink with the study: about 5 in every 100 dead-end ideas still pass. Real effects, though, get caught far less often. True 'yes' results thin out while the false ones stay.
A study this small for the effect it hunts is called underpowered. Notice that the whole curve dropped, not just the dot. Low power hurts in every field, whatever its odds.
Now go back to 100 per group but make the effect faint. Power is about 11% and a 'yes' is true about 35% of the time. A faint effect hurts in exactly the same way, because both work through power.
Keep the faint effect but run 1,000 per group. Power climbs back to about 61% and a 'yes' is true about 75% of the time. A big enough study can make up for a faint effect.

Finally, push to the strongest study: it catches nearly every real effect. The curve rises above the dashed yardstick, but the dot stops near 83%. With 1 true idea for every 4 false ones, even perfect power can't pass that ceiling.

understand.explanation: A study that is small, or that hunts a faint effect, catches fewer of the real effects: its power drops. False alarms don't drop with it, because about 5 in every 100 dead-end ideas still pass the test. So a bigger share of the 'yes' results are false alarms, and the chance that any given 'yes' is true (PPV) falls. Ioannidis derives this from his PPV formula, shows it in figure panels at power 0.20, 0.50 and 0.80, and states it as Corollaries 1 and 2: fields with small studies or small effects should expect fewer true findings. This is an argument from the formula, not a measurement across fields. The paper also notes the factors interact: fields that expect small effects may run larger studies to make up for it.
understand.quote: The smaller the studies conducted in a scientific field, the less likely the research findings are to be true. Small sample size means smaller power and, for all functions above, the PPV for a true research finding decreases as power decreases towards 1 − β = 0.05.

connect.caption: This is the paper's formula for one study with no bias. (1 − β) is the power, the share of real effects caught; in the model it comes from the people-per-group and effect-size sliders. β is the share missed. R is the field's true-to-false ratio (the odds slider), and α = 0.05 is the false-alarm rate. The bottom equals (1 − β)R + α, so as power shrinks toward α, the true 'yes' results shrink while the false alarms (α) stay put.

concepts.recap: Small studies and faint effects both lower power. Since false alarms don't shrink with power, a 'yes' from a weak study is less likely to be true.

activities.prompt: The paper contrasts big trials in cardiology (several thousand people) with molecular studies about 100-fold smaller. Here both hunt the same small effect in a field with the same odds. The equal effects and odds are our assumption. A third case adds a large effect, like smoking's link to cancer, in a small study.

cases.label: Large cardiology-style trial: 2,000 per group, small effect
Small molecular-style study: 20 per group, same small effect
Small study, but a large effect (illustrative size)

activities.takeaway: With everything else equal, the big trial's 'yes' is true about 83% of the time and the small study's only about a third of the time. A large effect lets even a small study do well, because it lifts power. Those are Corollaries 1 and 2 seen as one movement of the curve. These numbers are illustrative; the paper gives the sample-size contrast, not these exact values.

concepts.title: Bending the analysis turns 'no' into 'yes'
concepts.idea: Bias (u), the share of analyses that should have been negative but get reported as findings, adds false 'yes' results and lowers PPV.

predict.question: A field keeps bending its analyses just as often as before, but it starts running much bigger studies, so power rises a lot. What happens to the chance that one of its 'yes' results is true?
options: It rises a little, but the bending still holds it well down
It jumps close to 100%, because big studies catch real effects
It stays exactly the same, because only the bending matters
It falls, because bigger studies find more false effects
why: Right. More power adds a few more true 'yes' results. The bent 'yes' results from false ideas stay, so they keep the chance well below what an honest study would give.

Tempting, because power did help in the last concept. But bending makes false ideas come out 'yes' whatever the sample size, so a huge study still carries those false alarms (in the walkthrough, about 32%).
Bending is the main drag, but power still counts. Catching more real effects adds true 'yes' results, so the chance does creep up.
The paper does warn that extremely large studies can flag trivial effects. That is a different problem. In this model more power only adds true 'yes' results, so the chance cannot fall.

terms.means: The share of analyses that should have come out 'no' but get reported as findings anyway, because of bias
Splitting the data into groups after seeing the results, then checking each group until one shows an effect
Publishing only the analyses or outcomes that came out 'yes' and leaving out the rest

model.title: How often a 'yes' is true when some 'no' results get bent into 'yes'
model.note: Teaching model: power comes from a simple two-sided, two-group test with a false-alarm rate of 0.05. It uses the size of the real effect in standard-deviation units and the number of people per group. The chance a 'yes' is true uses the paper's single-study formula with bias (its Table 2). Like the paper, it assumes the same share of analyses is bent whether or not the idea is true. Reverse bias (true findings buried) and multiple teams are left out. The formula is the paper's. All slider settings and resulting numbers are illustrative, not the paper's data.

controls.label: True ideas per false idea tested (R)

outputs.label: Chance a 'yes' is true, if run honestly
Chance a 'yes' is true (PPV)
outputs.expr: (power * odds + u * (1 - power) * odds) / (power * odds + 0.05 + u * 0.95 + u * (1 - power) * odds)

x.label: True ideas per false idea tested (R)

series.label: This study, as reported
series.expr: (power * x + u * (1 - power) * x) / (power * x + 0.05 + u * 0.95 + u * (1 - power) * x)

steps.say: This is the same picture as before. The solid curve shows how often a 'yes' is true across fields, and the dot marks this field.
One new slider: the share of results that should have said 'no' but get reported as 'yes' because the analysis was bent. Watch the solid curve sink.
The dashed curve stays put. It is the same study run honestly, kept for comparison. The new box counts how many false ideas come out 'yes'.

explore.prompt: Bend the analysis yourself. Find out how little bending it takes to spoil a 'yes', and what can still rescue one.

goals.text: Starting from the original study, add just enough bending that a 'yes' becomes slightly worse than a coin flip: true less than 50% of the time, but more than 45%.
hints: Only one slider adds false 'yes' results without changing the study itself.
Small amounts matter. Nudge the bending slider up from zero and watch the PPV box, not the curve.
The tipping point comes well before one in five 'no' results gets bent.

goals.text: Leave heavy bending in place, with at least 30% of 'no' results reported as 'yes', and still get a 'yes' that is more likely true than false.
hints: Bigger studies alone won't get you there. What else made 'yes' results trustworthy in the earlier concepts?
Bending turns false ideas into 'yes' results. A field that tests fewer false ideas has fewer to bend.
Keep the bending slider at or above 30%, then move the true-ideas-per-false-idea slider well to the right.

feedback.correct: Yes. Extra power adds true 'yes' results, so the chance creeps up. The bent 'yes' results from false ideas don't depend on sample size, though, so the bending keeps the chance held down. The paper's own advice is that large studies may still have biases.
feedback.incorrect: You probably expected sample size to decide everything, either curing the problem or making it worse. In the paper's formula, bending adds false 'yes' results at the same rate whatever the study's size. More power helps a little, and only less bending removes those false alarms.

steps.say: Start honest, with nothing bent. The solid and dashed curves lie on top of each other, and a 'yes' in this field is true about 74% of the time.

Now bend one in ten analyses that should have said 'no'. The paper calls this share u. Ways to do it: a post hoc subgroup analysis (slicing data after seeing it) or selective reporting (publishing only what 'worked').
Look at the false-alarm box. Chance alone used to let 5% of false ideas through as 'yes'. Now it is nearly 15%: chance's 5% plus the bent ones.
At u = 0.2 the solid curve sinks well below the dashed honest one. A 'yes' is now true only about 40% of the time, so it is more likely false than true.
Bend half of them, and a 'yes' is true about 27% of the time. The idea had a 20% chance before anyone ran the study, so the study added almost nothing.
Can a huge study rescue it? With 2,000 people per group, power climbs to nearly 100%. Yet a 'yes' is true only about 32% of the time. More people don't stop false ideas from being bent into 'yes'.
Now undo the bending in the same big study. A 'yes' is true about 83% of the time. The drop from 83% to 32% was what the bending cost. The cure is less bending, not just more people.

understand.explanation: The paper defines bias as design, data, analysis or reporting choices that produce a 'finding' when an honest analysis would have said 'no'. It calls u the share of such analyses that get reported as findings anyway. Most honest 'no' results come from false ideas, so bending them adds mostly false 'yes' results. The false-alarm rate climbs from 5% toward 5% + u, and the chance a 'yes' is true (PPV) falls. Ioannidis showed this by adding u to his 2 × 2 table (Table 2) and plotting PPV against pre-study odds for several levels of u at three levels of power (Figure 1). This is a model built on assumptions, not a measurement. It assumes u is the same for true and false ideas, it leaves out 'reverse bias' (true findings buried), which the paper thinks is less common, and the drop fails only if a study catches real effects no more often than its 5% false-alarm rate.
understand.quote: In the presence of bias (Table 2), one gets PPV = ([1 - β]R + uβR)/(R + α − βR + u − uα + uβR), and PPV decreases with increasing u, unless 1 − β ≤ α, i.e., 1 − β ≤ 0.05 for most situations. Thus, with increasing bias, the chances that a research finding is true diminish considerably.

connect.caption: This is the paper's PPV formula with bias. 1 − β is power (the orange-linked output), R is the true-to-false ratio (green slider) and α is the 0.05 false-alarm rate. u (the bending slider) appears in both parts. In the top, uβR counts real effects that were missed but bent into 'yes'. In the bottom, u − uα counts false ideas bent into 'yes', which is why bending drags PPV down. Set u to 0 and you get back the honest formula from earlier concepts.

concepts.recap: Every analysis bent from 'no' to 'yes' mostly adds a false finding, so more flexibility means a 'yes' is less likely true, and bigger studies can't wash that out.

activities.title: What pushes u up?
activities.prompt: Sort each research practice by what it does. Does it bend more 'no' results into 'yes' (raises u), does it hold bending down, or is it plain chance, which is not bias at all?

cards.text: After seeing the results, the team checks men, women, older and younger patients separately, and reports the group that shows an effect
cards.feedback: This is a post hoc subgroup analysis, which the paper lists as a way to make more relationships cross p = 0.05.

cards.text: Partway through, the team changes what counts as having the disease
cards.feedback: The paper names 'changes in the disease or control definitions' as a form of manipulation that raises u.

cards.text: Some patients are dropped from the data after the team looks at how they did
cards.feedback: The paper calls this 'serendipitous inclusion or exclusion of certain patients or controls': flexibility that raises u.

cards.text: The team tries many analysis methods and reports only the one with the best result
cards.feedback: This is selective reporting. The paper warns about fields where 'only “best” results are reported'.

cards.text: A funder who profits from a positive result helps design and write up the study
cards.feedback: The paper's Corollary 5 says conflicts of interest may increase bias, u.

cards.text: The plan is written and registered before any data come in, and the study follows it to the letter
cards.feedback: The paper suggests upfront registration and adhering to a protocol, as in randomized trials, to diminish bias.

cards.text: The outcome is one everyone agrees on and can't be redefined, such as death
cards.feedback: The paper says true findings may be more common when outcomes are 'unequivocal and universally agreed (e.g., death)'.

cards.text: A flawlessly run study of a false idea gets p < 0.05 purely by luck
cards.feedback: The paper says bias 'should not be confused with chance variability'. This false alarm is already counted in the 5% α, not in u.

activities.takeaway: Flexibility after seeing the data, and interests in a particular answer, push u up. Fixed plans and agreed outcomes hold it down. Some false 'yes' results happen by luck even in perfect studies; those are α, not bias.

concepts.title: When nothing is there, effects measure bias
concepts.idea: In a field where no tested effect is real, every claimed effect comes from chance plus bias, so the size of the claimed effects measures the field's bias.

terms.means: A research field where none of the effects being tested is actually real
How many times more likely an outcome is in one group than in another; 1.0 means no difference
The overall push toward 'yes' results in a field once all its biases are added together

concepts.recap: If nothing real is there, chance alone scatters results around zero, so any steady, one-sided pattern of claimed effects measures bias, and very large effects deserve suspicion before celebration.

understand.explanation: Imagine a field where none of the ideas being tested is real; the paper calls this a “null field.” If its studies were perfect, their estimates would only scatter by chance around 'no effect': a relative risk (how many times more often the outcome happens in one group than in another, where 1.0 means no difference) would land a little above or a little below 1.0, and about 1 test in 20 would reach p < 0.05 by luck (the false-alarm rate α). Bias is the share u of analyses that should have come out negative but get reported as findings, and it pushes results one way, so any steady excess beyond that chance scatter is not a discovery but a reading of the field's net bias, meaning all its biases added together. The paper goes further: among null fields, the ones claiming the biggest effects have the worst bias, so a very large, very significant effect calls for careful checking, not only excitement. This is a line of reasoning, not a measurement: in practice we rarely know for sure that a field is null, and the paper offers it as a way to read evidence, not as data from a real field.
understand.quote: In such a “null field,” one would ideally expect all observed effect sizes to vary by chance around the null in the absence of bias. The extent that observed findings deviate from what is expected by chance alone would be simply a pure measure of the prevailing bias.
understand.quote_where: Section 'Claimed Research Findings May Often Be Simply Accurate Measures of the Prevailing Bias'

activities.prompt: Follow the paper's own thought experiment about diet and a tumour. The paper itself says 'let us suppose': this is an imagined field, not real data. Reveal one stage at a time.

stages.label: 1. Assume nothing is real
stages.text: Suppose that no nutrient or eating pattern actually changes the risk of developing one particular tumour. Every nutrient you might test has no true effect. This is a null field.

stages.label: 2. A way to state the size of an effect
stages.text: Researchers compare people who eat the most of a nutrient (the top third of intake) with people who eat the least (the bottom third). The result is given as a relative risk. A relative risk of 1.0 means the two groups get the tumour equally often. A value of 1.3 means the high-intake group gets it 30% more often, and 0.8 means 20% less often.

stages.label: 3. What chance alone would give
stages.text: If the studies were flawless, each estimate would land somewhere near 1.0 by chance: some a bit above, some a bit below. Roughly 1 test in 20 would reach significance by luck, and those flukes would point in either direction. Nothing would line up.

stages.label: 4. What the literature claims
stages.text: Now suppose the published papers have tested 60 nutrients and report that every one of them is linked to the tumour, with relative risks between 1.2 and 1.4. That is far more 'findings' than chance allows, and they all point the same way.

stages.label: 5. The gap is the bias
stages.text: Since nothing real is there, the distance between stage 3 and stage 4 cannot be discovery. It can only come from bias: choices in design, analysis and reporting that turn 'no' into 'yes'. The size of the claimed effects is then a measure of the field's net bias, meaning all its biases added together. In the paper's words, claimed effect sizes are 'the most accurate estimates of the net bias'.

stages.label: 6. The twist, and its limits
stages.text: Comparing null fields, the ones claiming stronger effects are the ones with worse bias. The paper notes that a few true effects hidden among the false ones would not change this picture much when most findings are false. But we rarely know for certain that a field is null. The paper says researchers will resist that label, and that other lines of evidence or new methods are what eventually settle it.

activities.takeaway: When the truth is 'nothing', chance gives a scatter centred on no effect. Any steady, one-sided excess in what gets claimed is a reading of bias.

activities.title: Chance or bias?
activities.prompt: Picture an imagined null field: none of the effects tested is real. Sort each observation by what most likely produced it.

cards.text: Across many studies, the estimates fall a little above and a little below 'no effect'
cards.feedback: This is exactly what flawless studies produce when nothing is real: random scatter centred on no effect.

cards.text: About 1 test in 20 reaches p < 0.05
cards.feedback: That matches the false-alarm rate α = 0.05. Even perfect studies let this many flukes through.

cards.text: The few significant results are split between 'raises risk' and 'lowers risk'
cards.feedback: Chance has no favourite direction, so flukes point both ways. A split like this is what luck looks like.

cards.text: All 60 nutrients tested are reported as linked to the disease
cards.feedback: Chance would give about 3 lucky hits out of 60, not 60. A hit rate this high in a null field points to bias turning negatives into findings.

cards.text: The reported effects cluster tightly between 1.2 and 1.4, and none sits near 1.0
cards.feedback: Chance would put most estimates near 1.0. A tight one-sided cluster away from 1.0 is the paper's picture of the field's net bias.

cards.text: An effect appears only after some patients are dropped from the analysis after the data were seen
cards.feedback: The paper lists this kind of selective inclusion or exclusion as one way to push results over the p = 0.05 line. It is bias, not luck.

cards.text: Only the analyses that crossed p < 0.05 were written up; the others stayed in a drawer
cards.feedback: Selective reporting is the paper's typical example of bias. It fills the published record with 'yes' results that chance alone would not supply.

activities.takeaway: Chance looks like scatter, about α of tests reaching significance, and no favoured direction. Bias looks like too many findings, all leaning the same way.

activities.question: In a field where most ideas tested are long shots, a new study reports that one food triples the risk of a disease, with an extremely small p-value. What does the paper's argument suggest you should do first?

options.text: Treat it as a major discovery, because an effect this big and this significant is hard to get by luck
options.feedback: This is the traditional reading that the paper sets out to reverse. Luck rarely produces such an effect, but bias can. In low-odds fields, too large and too significant effects 'may actually be more likely to be signs of large bias'.

options.text: Look hard for what might have gone wrong in the data, analysis or reporting before believing it
options.feedback: Correct. The paper says such effects should lead investigators to 'careful critical thinking about what might have gone wrong'. That is a call for scrutiny, not an automatic verdict.

options.text: Conclude that the finding is certainly false
options.feedback: This goes too far. The argument makes bias a likely explanation that must be checked, not a proof. A few true effects can exist even in low-odds fields, and only further evidence can tell them apart.

options.text: Ignore the size of the effect, since only the p-value matters
options.feedback: The paper argues the reverse. The size and pattern of claimed effects carry information, possibly about bias, and the paper warns against reading research through p-values alone.

hints: In a field with few real effects, what is the most common source of an impressive-looking 'yes'?
The paper says this concept 'totally reverses' how we usually react to large effects. Which option is the reversed reaction, without overclaiming?

concepts.title: More teams racing, less trustworthy winners
concepts.idea: When n independent teams test the same question and attention goes to any one that reaches significance, the chance that this finding is true falls as n grows.

predict.question: A news story says one lab found that a common spice prevents a rare illness, which is a long-shot idea. Later you learn that 25 other labs quietly ran the same test and found nothing. Before, you thought this lab was the only one. How should you rate its 'yes' now?
options: Less likely to be true than you first thought
More likely to be true, because 26 labs studied it
Just as likely, because each lab's result stands on its own p-value
More likely, as long as that lab's study was very large
why: Right. With 26 labs testing a long-shot idea, a fluke 'yes' from at least one of them is very likely, so the one 'yes' that made the news counts for much less.
It feels as if more research should mean more certainty. But the other 25 labs' silence is not support. Their tests were extra chances for a fluke, and only the winner got noticed.
The lab's own p-value doesn't change. But the chance that a 'yes' is true depends on how many tries came before it. One hit out of 26 tries is far weaker than one hit out of one.
A big study helps catch real effects, but it doesn't remove the other labs' chances of a fluke. In the model, making studies bigger barely moves the dot once many teams are racing.

terms.means: Groups that each run their own separate study, so one team's luck has no effect on another's
An area of research where many teams are chasing the same questions at the same time

model.title: How often a winning 'yes' is true when several teams test the same question
model.note: Teaching model: power comes from a simple two-group test (two-sided, false-alarm rate 0.05), using the real effect's size in standard-deviation units and the number of people per group. The chance a 'yes' is true uses the paper's formula for several separate studies of equal power on the same question, where a 'yes' means at least one team reached significance. Bias is left out, as in the paper's version of this formula. Every team is assumed to have the same power. The R slider stops at 0.01, far above the paper's genome example (1 in 10,000), so the model's numbers differ from the paper's Box 1. The formula is the paper's. All slider settings and resulting numbers are illustrative, not the paper's data.

controls.label: True ideas per false idea tested (R)

outputs.label: Real effects caught by one team (power)
Chance a winning 'yes' is true (PPV)
outputs.expr: odds * (1 - pow(max(0, 1 - power), teams)) / (odds + 1 - pow(0.95, teams) - odds * pow(max(0, 1 - power), teams))

outputs.label: Chance some team gets a fluke 'yes' when nothing is there

x.label: True ideas per false idea tested (R)

series.label: A winning 'yes' with this many teams
series.expr: x * (1 - pow(max(0, 1 - power), teams)) / (x + 1 - pow(0.95, teams) - x * pow(max(0, 1 - power), teams))

series.label: The same study done by one team alone

steps.say: Same picture as before. The solid curve and the dot show how often a 'yes' turns out true. The sliders set study size, effect size and how many tested ideas are true.
One new slider: how many teams test the very same question. Each team runs its own study, and the news reports whichever team gets a 'yes'.
Two dashed curves help you compare: one team on its own, and the chance before any study. Watch where the solid curve heads as more teams join.

explore.prompt: Race some teams. First find when a winning 'yes' stops being trustworthy, then find what can rescue it.

goals.text: Leave the field and the studies as they start. Add teams until a winning team's 'yes' is more likely false than true.
hints: Which slider gives a fluke more chances to show up?
Add teams one at a time and watch the dot sink toward the 'as likely true as false' line.
It tips over somewhere between five and ten teams.

goals.text: Imagine at least ten teams racing. Make a winning team's 'yes' more likely true than false again.
hints: Try making each study bigger first. Does the dot climb much?
With many teams, extra flukes are the problem. Only a field where more of the tested ideas are true gives real effects enough weight.
Slide the true-to-false ideas slider right in small steps and stop when the dot rises above the dashed line.

feedback.correct: Yes. The 25 silent labs were 25 more chances for a fluke. With that many tries on a long-shot idea, a false 'yes' from somebody is close to expected, so the one that made the news is weak evidence.
feedback.incorrect: It's natural to think more research means more reliable findings. But when only the team that says 'yes' gets noticed, every extra team adds another chance of a false alarm. A real effect can be caught at most once in a meaningful sense, so as teams multiply, flukes take up a bigger share of the 'yes' results.

steps.say: Start with one team in the field from before. Its 'yes' is true about 74% of the time, up from 20% before the study.
Now three teams test the same question. Each has a 5% chance of a false alarm, so the chance that somebody gets a fluke 'yes' rises to about 14%. The winning 'yes' drops to about 62% true.

Ten teams. These are independent teams: each runs its own study, so each has its own shot at a fluke. Some team now has about a 40% chance of a fluke 'yes', and a winning 'yes' is only about 38% true.

Can bigger studies fix it? Give every team 1,000 people per group. Power jumps to nearly 100%, yet the winning 'yes' barely moves. Some team was already catching the real effects. The extra flukes are what hurt.

Now a long-shot field: about one true idea for every hundred false ones, back to normal studies, one team. A single 'yes' makes the idea about ten times more believable than before, from about 1% to about 10%.
Ten teams chase the same long shot. The winning 'yes' is now only about 2.4% likely true, about two and a half times the starting guess.

Twenty teams: this is a hot field. The solid curve has sunk nearly onto the 'before any study' curve. The published 'yes' is about 1.5% likely true against 1% before, hardly more believable than the idea was before anyone studied it at all.

understand.explanation: When several separate teams test the same question, each has its own 5% chance of a false alarm, so the chance that somebody gets a fluke 'yes' climbs fast: about 40% with ten teams. The chance that someone catches a real effect also rises, but it can't pass 100%, and decent studies are already close. So if attention goes to whichever team says 'yes', that 'yes' is more and more often a fluke. The paper builds this into its 2 × 2 table for n studies of equal power and shows in Figure 2 that PPV falls as n grows. In its genome example (Box 1), ten teams leave a significant hit at only about 1.5 in 10,000, against 1 in 10,000 before any study. This version assumes no bias, equal power and fully separate teams. The paper also notes that a hot field can sometimes push for larger studies and better standards, and that the cure is to weigh all the evidence, not one team's hit.
understand.quote: The hotter a scientific field (with more scientific teams involved), the less likely the research findings are to be true. This seemingly paradoxical corollary follows because, as stated above, the PPV of isolated findings decreases when many teams of investigators are involved in the same field.

check.task: Show that strong studies don't rescue a long-shot hot field. Use studies that catch at least 90% of real effects, in a field with at most one true idea for every 20 false ones tested. Make a winning 'yes' less than twice as believable as the idea was before any study.
check.hint: Raise power with the study size, make the field a long shot, then remember that each extra team is one more chance for a fluke.
check.misconception: More teams studying a question means more evidence, so any one team's 'yes' must be more reliable, especially if the studies are big.

connect.caption: The paper's formula for n equal-power studies, no bias. Its n is the Teams slider, not people per group. R is the true-to-false ideas slider. β is 1 minus one team's power, so β^{n} is the chance every team misses a real effect. With α = 0.05, 1 − (1 − α)^{n} is the chance some team gets a fluke 'yes' (the fluke box). As n grows, that part swells in the bottom of the fraction and PPV sinks.

concepts.recap: When many teams chase the same question and only the 'yes' gets noticed, that 'yes' is worth less. In a long-shot field, it is barely more believable than the idea was before anyone looked.
